utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in the courtroom and to those who are listening to these procedures. Mr. Tolimir, you -- the witness should be brought in, please, and then you may continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Take your earphones, please, so that I can address you. Good afternoon, sir. Welcome back to the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I have to remind you that the affirmation to tell the truth you made at the beginning of your testimony still applies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir is continuing his cross-examination. Mr. Tolimir, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. May God's peace reign in this house and may God's will, not mine, be done in these proceedings. And I also want to welcome Dr. Petrovic again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us continue. We had a few questions left. It is unfortunate that you had to stay just forever that, but I'm sure that the Prosecutor will have some questions for you as well. Yesterday on page 45, today it's 14427 to 429 [Realtime transcript read in error "2429"], you spoke about Colonel Bunel. You said that he's an officer of the French intelligence service and that he told you some information about activities he had observed in Tuzla in relation to how American soldiers were treating Muslims. Could you please tell us whether there were other journalists there who saw this, did he find that out from others about the situation, and was it even allowed to write and talk about this event?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, sir, as I was saying yesterday, it's -- it was an interview that was published in magazine "Europa" in 2006; that was my second conversation with him two years prior to that. I also interviewed him in Paris and that was also published. And then for the second interview I sent my questions to him by Internet and in response he was informing me that - and you will understand it, of course, because you're also an intelligence officer - he informed me that there were no journalists. And I'm sure that if he would be summoned here, he would repeat that story. I also promised the Prosecutor that upon my return to Belgrade I will send the French part of the text -- oh, I can send the entire text, but this part where events in Tuzla are discussed. And I must say, Mr. Bunel could not take part. Even the English officers were not allowed to be present at interrogation of the completely exhausted soldiers who managed to get to Tuzla after several months and then were transferred to the United States.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, I would like to ask you to slow down while reading. You are very fast, and it is very problematic for the interpreters to catch everything you were talking. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. President. On page 2, line 2, references were wrongly written. The main -- the direct interrogation, the direct examination, pages were 14427 to 14429.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that clarification. This should remind you, Mr. Tolimir, to slow down while referring to a page number. It's always very difficult to catch that. Now please continue, and try to avoid overlapping.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Dr. Petrovic, could you also send the same document not only to the Prosecutor but also to the Chamber and myself, this document, because it was discussed here in the proceedings. You told us that these people went to the United States to a city called Richmond. Did I get that right? And do you have any further information about it? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before I answer, I first of all want to apologise to the Presiding Judge and the interpreters. I will do my best to slow down. The information, various information, I received only later from people from the diaspora who lived in Richmond at the time, and I managed to reconstruct the situation basing it on the time when Izetbegovic soldiers first reached Tuzla and then went to the United States. I managed to conclude that these are most probably the said fighters. Unfortunately, General, sir, no one from Republika Srpska, from your army, wanted to assist us and send a cameraman and a journalist to do some investigative journalism and show images or footage of all these events. I am certain about the correctness of this piece of information, but I did not see those people who are there. Bunel told me that after interrogating them, the Americans transferred those people to the United States, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Petrovic. Could you please tell us whether Bunel, at the time when the men were being interrogated in Tuzla and their departure later for United States, was Bunel at the time an active officer of the French intelligence service? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, sir, yes. He was active-duty military intelligence officer until he was arrested for allegedly assisting the Serbs. This was -- this arrest was a premeditated arrest by the French government because later on he was rehabilitated and got a job as a commentator on French state radio but did not return to active-duty service. So this was in 1996, in spring of 1996, the events he told me about. And then for the next three years he was still intelligence colonel of the French army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have in e-court 1D77.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And then I'll put a question to you. We'll wait for the document. Thank you. [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you need your microphone. Otherwise, you will not be recorded.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We can now see 1D77. Please, Dr. Petrovic, take a look at what's on the screen and tell me, is this the text you told us about and that you had published in magazine "Europa"? And is this a reflection of the words of Mr. Bunel?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, sir, your team is very quick and Internet makes it possible. Yes, this paragraph was on the Internet. I know that. And this is one segment of the interview conducted with Colonel Bunel. And let me correct myself immediately. It was published in Europa in 2005, it seems here. I still believe it was in 2006, but it is possible that it was published in 2005. I don't have the text here on me. And I made it in late 2004. This is most probably correct, but it's just a technical error. My apologies, I promised I would send the entire text to all the parties upon my return to Belgrade. I do not have it here, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Petrovic. So this is an excerpt from this text. I would be grateful if you would send all the parties the entire text.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document until we have the entire text, and then we can move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Is this the only page of this document, Mr. Tolimir? Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. This document consists of only one page. There is a translation of the document. I have it in e-court. I don't know why it is not on the screen. We can check that later, of course. I would like to remind you that the document was used during cross-examination of Mr. Jean-Rene Ruez.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, with your leave, the document that is attached to this original one, the translation, needs to be released only in e-court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And this is an obligation of the Defence. We await with our decision until we have seen the translation. You may continue, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Dr. Petrovic, yesterday, on page 14459 to 460, you told us that bin Laden was observed in Sarajevo. And you mentioned the name of a female journalist, but we didn't see the surname in the transcript. You said the name was Renata, but not the surname. Could you please tell us what year was it, and what was the name, the full name, of the journalist, and who -- which journalists were those who saw bin Laden drinking coffee on Igman?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, first of all, let me apologise to the Presiding Judge because when mentioning the name yesterday, I mentioned - and later on I was sorry but now I have a chance to correct this - that this was a reporter for Stern, but she was actually working for Der Spiegel and she was the famous reporter, at least in our country, for many years for Der Spiegel from Yugoslavia, and it's Renate Flottau [Realtime transcript read in error "Vlottau"]; that is her name. In my book, I quote her, the book which I also mentioned during yesterday's examination. "Al-Qaeda and the Green Comintern Against the Judeo-Christian Civilisation," published in 2002 in Belgrade. I had heard this before, and she admitted that while waiting on two consecutive days for President Izetbegovic on the premise of his offices in the Presidency in Sarajevo during the war, she saw there bin Laden whom she described in the following terms: She had the impression that he was another silly type, and you could see many of these during the war who had come from all parts of the world. And she didn't pay much attention to his story at the time, but she said that she knew that this was Osama bin Laden, who, having arrived to the office and having entered the room where Mr. Izetbegovic was, could perhaps be the best illustration of what I know about Islamism in the territory of the former Yugoslavia and about which no Western journalists practically ever talked about, except in some -- on some rare occasions. I wish to repeat once again a very important detail in connection with this, something else that can be found in my book. Mrs. Flottau says that she did not consider it important to write a text or make an interview with him and that even had she done that, the then editors would not have published that. I remember her telling this to me personally. And as for Izetbegovic, he probably discussed the El Mujahid brigade with him which was a well-known spear-head unit which was financed by Osama bin Laden during the war in Bosnia. The name of al-Qaeda was not used in public at the time. Not yet. However, the group was already operational and Osama bin Laden had some bases in Albania. There is proof about this, the Americans know it, all intelligence services of the world know the information that as many as 500 men were ready at any given time at the training camp in Albania and later on for the events in Kosova and Metohija. I could talk a lot about that, but let me not keep you with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Petrovic. Can you please check whether the name of Ms. Renate Flottau has been correctly transcribed in the record, and can you tell us which year she talked about when she said that Osama bin Laden had visited Mr. Izetbegovic in Sarajevo, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember whether it was 1993 or 1994. But at the time, from the beginning of the war and onwards, there were many from Saudi Arabia, as the Croatians can confirm today, used to arrive into Bosnia mainly via Split. There were many Islamic volunteers, the Afghan fighters, under quotation marks, as they are sometimes called, used to enter Bosnia through Croatian in order to fight the Serbs. There is a lot of evidence about that today, but that is not directly the subject that we're dealing with here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Would you please look at page 8, line 9, and check if this is the right spelling of the family name of Ms. Flottau. Or do you know the correct spelling?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just let me -- it's spelt with an F rather than with a V. Flottau, F-l-o-t-a-u [as interpreted]. F like "Frankreich."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Petrovic. Please, as this is radical fighting Islam, and you said that in Podravanje in 1993 a man was roasted on the spit, a Serbian soldier, you said that on page 43 of the transcript, in line 25, can you please just tell us something about it, because you have written a book about al-Qaeda. Can you tell us something about the radical combat Islamic morale during the war in Bosnia, which surfaced in the territory, if you wrote about that in your book. You probably know this and then you could tell us something and then later on I might ask additional questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, first of all, another clarification about the man who was roasted on the spit. I never saw that. I saw a photograph which I published in a book, a book dealing with the beginnings of the war in Bosnia. And this remains etched on my memory. I think that the date is the 29th of August, 1992, and that this happened in the village Podravanje, in the vicinity of Srebrenica. I'm not even certain whether that man had been a soldier, but maybe just an inhabitant of that place, born in 1958 and killed in a most horrible manner imaginable today. It's something that entails reviving methods of warfare from medieval times or even earlier. It was an act committed by one of these Afghan fighters, under quotation marks. So the most seasoned fighters for UMA, that's the international Islamic community. This is the UMA of Osama bin Laden and Iman Auzaba Hiri [phoen], his ideologue, as I described in my book. It means that there can be no agreement with Christians, no agreement with the Jews, but, rather, eternal struggle against him until UMA is to be established on the entire planet. It's a utopian concept, but it provides sufficient motive for new generations of young people throughout the world. And as I wrote in my book, and as I mentioned yesterday, this option Islamism is the line which resulted in Osama bin Laden having become their Che Guevara, which he has been for a number of years now. The force of the name is similar among the youngest generation of Muslims from Indonesia through to Bosnia. In order to show how important and decisive this is, and it follows from all the analyses of the civil war, I will provide an example and you will know better than me, General. August and September 1994, or is it 1995? - please help me - the bombing of Ozren which lasted for about two weeks and this was carried out by the NATO pact. The Serbian fighters had secured and entrenched themselves well in Ozren, and it was not possible to approach them. They, under quotation marks, resolved the situation but using NATO aircraft, after which -- and they were using depleted uranium bombs similar to those which were used when bombing the FR Yugoslavia in 1999, so it had already been used earlier in Bosnia and you know in how many places. And what followed then was the perverse finale of the operation when the members of the El Mujahid brigade which was financed and whose superior commander was Osama bin Laden finished the job and killed the survivors, cut off their heads. There is a video-tape which the Americans broadcast for the first time only after 9/11, that is to say, after the catastrophe in New York City. They did not want to broadcast this earlier. You can see the heads rolling and the propaganda action filmed by El Mujahid. Just imagine the NATO pact cooperating with the El Mujahid brigade in the Ozren brigade. Hardly anyone could deny what I have just said today. It's interesting for the Prosecution and for the Bench, General, that there were many similar situations where Serbs used to hide in the Communist manner by saying that everything is a military secret. I have friends -- I have a friend who is a doctor and whose brother had gone missing, and to this day it is not known that he has gone missing but it is known that these were one of the major losses of the Serbian army in this war. And your army and your Presidency never talked much about that, though it is logical that the whole planet should know something about this. But that's a quite different issue. Though, for me it is also a form of perversity. They throw uranium at you, they bomb you with it, and you keep silent about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Mindua has a question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Witness. What you're saying is, of course, very important. You wrote a book, furthermore, on that, specifically on the arrival of Mr. Osama bin Laden in Bosnia, and you wrote a book on the Mujahedins. But we are at a Tribunal here, so I would like to know if you yourself, if you have seen Osama bin Laden with these Mujahedins, or is what you're saying is something that you can state only following what you heard from the reporter Renate - I'm looking for the last name - Flottau; I don't know if I pronounced it correctly. Because we cannot just rely on hearsay here on that matter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, when Mrs. Flottau stated that, and she said it many times and publicly, it's as if I had seen it myself. She has a very good credibility. She's been a reporter for many decades. She was a correspondent for many, many years in the former Yugoslavia. She was working for a world-class weekly called Der Spiegel --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... you got a question by Judge Mindua: Did you see Osama bin Laden with the Mujahedins yourself, or did you hear it from another person? You answered that you heard something from Ms. Flottau. Could you please answer the question: Did you see Osama bin Laden yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course not. In that case, I would have made am interview with him. Every reporter in the world wanted to interview him. So, no, I have not seen him with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... that was enough. That was the question, and Judge Mindua should continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, very well. Thank you very much. That clarifies that. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I would like to inform you that the translation, the English translation, of the document 1D77 is now available in e-court. You may use it if you are interested in it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. As we used it, perhaps the witness could just glance at it once again and then if it could be admitted, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is the text. It is just my mistake that it was earlier than I seemed to have remembered. I thought it was published in March 2006, but it says here ... so I will check in Belgrade what date it was, but this is it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 1D77 shall be assigned Exhibit D266. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir. Sorry, I didn't see you, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you. And good afternoon to you, Mr. President, and everyone. Mr. President, it's unclear to me what -- I see that this was an excerpt of an article. I don't know that we have the entirety of the article in evidence. I'm not sure. I don't believe that we do. And to the extent that we don't, I'm not sure if -- I'm not sure where this emerges from or what part or amount of the article is missing because I think that's important, to place its context in the proper -- to frame it appropriately, I think, and put it in its proper context. Perhaps the witness can give us some information on that, on what part of the article this is. But from what I could read just a moment ago, it appears to be -- what we have now in e-court appears to be the words of the witness himself, talking about the information that he's received, but it's not clear what the source of the information is, when it was acquired, and all of those kinds of things. So maybe General Tolimir can elicit that from the witness, but I think that that's essential in order to -- in order for the Court to properly consider its probative nature and its weight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: To clarify the situation, we received this document as an exhibit, which doesn't say anything about the weight the Chamber will give to this document at the end of this trial. We have heard some comments from the witness. He said that this is part of the interview with Mr. Bunel. I have no idea which part of it. We don't see the -- we don't have the full text. We will see what will happen with that. Mr. Tolimir, you should, -- if you want, if you wish, you should clarify this with the witness or carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The witness said that he would send both to the accused and the Trial Chamber and the Prosecution the whole interview with Mr. Bunel, so I would just ask him to tell us now whether he has any knowledge of whether, on the lists in Potocari, the lists of those who were dead, included some persons who were actually alive and whether there was any information about that in the media that he was aware of in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Because he said that maybe some of these persons who are on the lists of the killed persons are still alive and are living in the city of Richmond in the United States. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This -- this question was not very clear. I would like to ask the witness: The text we have here on the screen, are these the words of Mr. Bunel to a question you put to him during the interview? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Mr. President. These are his words from a longer interview in which there was a lot of discussion about Islamism throughout the world and in Bosnia and assistance to the Islamists and Izetbegovic during the war by various organisations. And this is just the text which is directly linked to the Srebrenica events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. I just wanted to know if these words are the words of Mr. Bunel. Mr. Tolimir, you had a long question. You should rephrase it in order to receive a precise answer of this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I will rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Dr. Petrovic, do you know that the lists of persons who were killed in Potocari during the war in Srebrenica also include names of living persons who are alive but have been included in the lists as having been buried? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, sir, the Serbian public in Belgrade knows a lot about this. On several occasions, Mr. Bata Ivanisevic, who is at the head of the centre for the research of crimes against Serbs in the last civil war, provided examples. He made appearances on TV. He gave statements to the press. And I think it can be found through the services which you have available here at the Tribunal with examples of specific names of persons, whose names figure on the Muslim graveyard in Bratunac, were still alive. I don't know any specific names at this moment, but it is very easy to find this in documents. And, after all, you might contact Mr. Ivanisevic who could make a high quality witness as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, the name of the person you mentioned at the beginning of your answer was not recorded. Could you please repeat the name of that person.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. That is Mr. Bata Ivanisevic who, since 1992, has been investigating crimes and is particularly knowledgeable about the area of Podrinje. He perhaps has the best documentation about the crimes, including the names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I just asked for the name. Please focus on the question. Can you tell me, What is his function in this centre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Mr. Ivanisevic heads -- well, I don't know if his title is president, but he's the head of the centre for the investigations of crimes against Serbs in the war from 1992 to 1995 in Bosnia. The centre is located in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. With respect to the question that was put by General Tolimir, I take it he's referring to the book that he put into evidence by Mr. Ivanisevic. I don't know how many names the Defence alleges are names that appear on a burial list, but there's been no evidence in this case about names that appear on any burial list in Potocari. There's simply been no evidence of that. So to the extent that the question was framed in the context of names that have been identified that appear on a burial list for victims killed in Potocari, there's simply no evidence of that in the record for that comparison to have been made or to be appropriately put to the witness. That's the nature of the objection. We have the witness's answer, but I think it's important that the record reflect that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir, please move to your next question. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, just briefly. Perhaps it's a translation, perhaps an impreciseness in the phrasing. What was meant was the list of persons found in Potocari and not persons who were killed in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, is Bata the nickname of Mr. Ivanisevic? Is his real name Milivoj or something like that? Can you please tell us for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, his name is Milivoje Ivanisevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, yes, I can see that the name is recorded correctly now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Petrovic. Yesterday, on page 14459, you spoke about how these from Srebrenica who came to Tuzla went -- went to Richmond ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused please repeat the last part of the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, the interpreters asked you to repeat last part of the question. It was not translated.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you say yesterday, in the testimony relating to the Muslims from Srebrenica who were interviewed in Tuzla by Americans who were later taken to the city of Richmond, did you not say that many of them were probably on the missing persons lists? And this is something that you said yesterday on pages 17, lines 1 onwards.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think I said that. That would be a logical conclusion in view of the fact that I said that Colonel Bunel said that they had turned up at the American base in early spring 1996. So this is an interim of several months. By that time, more was known about the casualties. They didn't fit in anywhere. Either they were among the casualties, but they turned up with the Americans. I assume that they must have figured somewhere as casualties of war, military casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Petrovic. Yesterday when you were talking about Colonel Bunel, you said that bin Laden's Mujahedin were drinking coffee at Igman and that they were filmed. You said the French were helping them at the time. Can you please help us, who was helping whom? Was it the Mujahedin helping the French or the French helping the Mujahedin? This is on page 5 of the transcript, line 18 onwards.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, sir, during the war, I frequently worked with French television, TF1. This is the largest private TV station in Europe. This is how I made my living, because I was thrown out from all the media in Belgrade. And I heard this from one of the crews on one occasion when I was with them in Bosnia. I think it's sufficient if you and the Prosecution and the Trial Chamber is interested in checking this, then you could go and look at the documentation of TF1. I'm sure that this has not been deleted. There's footage of a check-point at Igman with French soldiers, Dutch soldiers sitting there, where you have seasoned Mujahedin turning up. Not local ones but international, seasoned ones. And there is a record of them sitting and drinking coffee with French and Dutch soldiers. And this is what the crew told me. I don't think that they lied to me. If they lied to me, then I am lying to you. This is not something that anybody would be willing to show just like that, but perhaps if you requested it they would be willing to show that to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please avoid overlapping. At this point in time, I would like to get a clarification from the witness. You said yesterday: "French television filmed them at a check-point near Igman where the Mujahedin are drinking coffee in the morning with French and Dutch soldiers." Can you -- have you seen that? Or what is the source of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it's clear from my testimony that I was not present and that this is a very convincing testimony by my colleagues from French television. I worked with a lot of crews during the war in Bosnia as their interpreter, and I don't remember receiving any information from them that was not correct. I'm not an eye-witness though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell me if you have seen this film the French crew has taken.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I did not see it personally, because this was not something that happened on the occasion when I was with them. Otherwise I would have seen it myself. This is something that happened with one of the previous crews. These are events that journalists remember, but obviously this was not broadcast, in the same way that the French at Majevica, and I referred to that in my previous testimony, gave military food rations to the same Mujahedin that I saw personally. Later the Serbs took that from the Mujahedin. The French NATO lunch rations, that's what they were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Dr. Petrovic, since you wrote your book al-Qaeda -- in the book al-Qaeda, did you cover how these fighters of bin Laden, so-called Mujahedin, were settling in Bosnian villages of Bioca, Maoca, villages where Serbs were expelled in Central Bosnia? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, General, sir. I did not cover that. I think this is a fact that turned up more even in the Bosnian press later, but it's a generally-known fact. I did mention that they were being issued passports, that bin Laden had a Bosnian passport, and that there were indications leading to fighters who were receiving passports of the new Bosnian state, and they turned up later in Zambia and some other countries. But I did not specifically mention that they had their own villages. Bioca, I think, was the name of that village. They still live there to this very day. But I think that I did not put that in the book, as far as I remember. This was in 2002.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, can you tell me what is the source of your knowledge about Bosnian passport issued for Osama bin Laden?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I really couldn't say. This is the result of various information compiled over a long period of time, even from the time when I was in the Bina news agency. There were plenty of Israeli sources for that, Israelis who were in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. That's absolutely sufficient. Thank you very much. Judge Nyambe has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Yes, on page 21, today's transcript, line 5, you have stated that they turned up later in Zambia and other countries and that they have their own villages. Can you amplify on that, exactly which part of Zambia they may be and which villages they occupied, if you know. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is a misunderstanding. Nobody said anything about villages in Zambia and Tanzania. My information indicated that the diplomatic services of the new Bosnian state concealed Islamists at some lower-ranking positions, bin Laden's people. Islamists, they were not noticeable because Bosnia is part of the non-aligned world, so it was easier to enter African and other countries that still remembered non-alignment. I spoke about Zambia and I think Tanzania also was something that I referred to in the context of two major operations where embassies were blown up. These were two major Islamists actions, and some Israeli and other experts consider that there were Mujahedin there or bin Laden's people who were actually concealed in these trade representative offices or diplomatic offices. This was something that can be described as white-collar al-Qaeda. This is what I meant. The villages that I mentioned were actually the villages in Bosnia where former fighters, Afghanistanis, settled. They got married, have children. They still live there. They put roots there. And in the Bosnian public, this is something that is discussed from time to time, the potential danger that is posed by these Mujahedin still today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you. Okay. I think, just for the record, since it's on record and since you link the al-Qaeda cells in Africa to embassies that were bombed in those countries, you probably mean Tanzania and Kenya, and not Zambia, because no embassy was bombed in Zambia in connection with al-Qaeda activities. Just for the record. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour. You are correct. Kenya and Tanzania and not Zambia. You are correct. It was a slip of the tongue. These are well-known bombings. The whole planet knows about that, but I misspoke.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In this Tribunal, we are dealing with events in the former Yugoslavia and not on other continents. Mr. Tolimir, can you help me? What is the purpose of this line of questions which take us far away from Srebrenica, Zepa, and other locations in the former Yugoslavia relevant to the indictment?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We began with a question on the -- the departure of people from Srebrenica to Richmond, a town in America, and through the answers of the witness we got to these questions. I was asking about Tuzla, about what Mr. Bunel saw, what he found out, and how the Americans concealed them and did not allow others to have interviews with them and then eventually they transferred them to United States. But they could actually be persons who are potentially on the lists of missing persons, and these lists of missing persons are figuring in this trial. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, at that point in time, you didn't receive any comment from the Chamber. But now we are talking about Osama bin Laden and bombing of embassies and so on. Please focus on this case and put questions that the witness can answer and provide the Chamber with his knowledge but related to the events we are dealing with in this trial.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I understood you well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, could you please tell us whether bin Laden's fighters, members of his so-called El Mujahid Unit, remained in Bosnia and Herzegovina and were they engaged in the war and were they present in the area of Srebrenica and Tuzla? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, sir, let me refer you to Mr. Joseph Bodansky, American and Israeli expert on terrorism. He wrote a lot about it. He is one of the foremost experts on this planet. And he published a book, even, in United States. He is an Israeli intelligence officer working in United States. He can confirm the presence of the El Mujahid brigade in various areas in Bosnia and Herzegovina. I first found out about that at Ms. Biljana Plavsic. She purchased the cassette, video cassette, from the Croats, and Carl Bildt was present in her office. He was writing notes for two hours about the video-tape. The name of the person is, I'll repeat it, Josep Bodansky. He is the foremost expert in the world on this topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, during the direct examination, you talked about geopolitics of energy. And on page 12, line 25, you told us that Kosovo has about 60 per cent of energetic resources of Serbia. You also gave us the figures in millions of tonnes. Immediately after that you were asked by the Prosecutor whether you express your own position in your book, and I would like to ask you whether this is it your personal opinion, namely that the 60 per cent of the Serbian resources are located in Kosovo, or was it something that you have on the basis of research? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, sir, I heard that information from several professors of the mining and geology school in Belgrade who are the foremost experts in the world for that topic. That's about -- there's about 20 billion tonnes of coal, not very high quality coal. But that's all we have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, what is the purpose of these questions about mines in Kosovo? You should use your time in cross-examination in a more efficient way.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, there was mention of wars, and there was mention of economic resources. The war in Kosovo was waged over economic resources. I'm entitled to ask the witness whether during his geopolitical research you came to a conclusion that wars are being waged over energetic and other economic resources.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: There are many reasons for wars in the world. This is not related to this case, Mr. Tolimir. You should use your time much more efficiently. Put questions in relation to the events mentioned in the indictment. Carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please, Dr. Petrovic, could you please tell us whether NATO got out of the European Union for the first time during the war in the Balkans; is that something you've learned through your research?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In geopolitics it's a well-known fact. The Americans, after the first war with Iraq, in 1993 and 1994, came to Dunav and also, for the first time, in 1999, they started building a base, Bondsteel, and it will be a strategically important start-off point towards Eurasia. That's a well-known fact. And as I already mentioned, wars are waged nowadays over resources, or experts for energy and almost important politicians will confirm that this is an absolute truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Petrovic. Could you please tell us whether bin Laden and his Mujahedin stay and have coffee in Sarajevo on Mount Igman in Bosnia if NATO alliance countries and UNPROFOR countries were against that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I think this is an inappropriate question to put to this witness. The witness, as he told us, is not an eye-witness. He, in fact, doesn't know anything, he can't know anything, about the background of the behaviour of NATO and UNPROFOR in relation to Mujahedins. He is a journalist. He is not an expert witness. He is a journalist. He was called for his testimony and his knowledge about the video shots we have seen in the courtroom. This is the reason why he is here, and he was asked during examination-in-chief about this. You should focus on the testimony of the witness during examination-in-chief. This is the scope of his examination and not his second-hand or third- or fourth-hand knowledge about possible reasons for actions taken by NATO or UNPROFOR. Please consider your line of questions again.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I can conclude my examination. However, yesterday, during the direct examination, on page 11, line 25, the witness answered the questions put to him by the Prosecutor in relation to geopolitics and energetics, what his field of expertise and research was, and this is why I'm asking this question. He told us that he is interested, and was interested, in geopolitics of food, water, energy, and so on. But if you disallow this line of questioning, I will not put those kind of questions anymore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed, you should put questions which has a value for your case, and not about geopolitical knowledge. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Dr. Petrovic, could you please tell us weather in the Balkans the geopolitics of water and other energetic such as the energy sources in Kosovo were the reason for all the wars in the region? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, sir, it's a well-known fact among people who deal in geopolitics, like everywhere else on our planet, it is something that is of great importance and something that major countries take into consideration when they are considering taking others -- other resources belonging to others. And if I may add one sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No. Sorry, I have to interrupt you. Mr. Tolimir, you got some guidance by me, and now you're, again, dealing with energy sources in Kosovo, and you get only the answer: "It's a well-known fact among people who deal with geopolitics ..." What kind of evidence is such an answer? It is a well-known fact. Everybody can read books and newspaper articles. This is not testimony about knowledge, personal knowledge and personal facts, and especially the lines of questions about energy and geopolitics. It is not helpful for your case. Please bear that in mind.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. In the indictment, I am charged with events in the war. I want to show that it's not the conflicting parties that were behind the war in Bosnia, but some other forces. If you don't want me to prove that, I will -- if you won't let me to do it, I will not have an opportunity and I won't do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, help me. How can you expect that this witness will be able to testify about this knowledge, about this fact, as he always answers in the way like he did with the last answer, "it is a well-known fact"? It is not helpful for your case to have a journalist to tell you anything about a well-known fact. This is it not evidence. Please continue your examination in a different way. You may -- you may -- we could have our first break now, then you may consider the situation with your Legal Advisor, and then we can continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. But this means that I'm not allowed to ask a journalist, and a researcher who was present there in the Balkans throughout the war, I cannot ask him anything about the causes of the war, and I am charged with elements of the war. We can ask him. We can now all see that the wars in Yugoslavia, in Iraq, in Libya, in Congo, are being waged in order to make a new distribution of resources of the non-allied countries which existed before but do not exist anymore. I just wanted to ask whether the war in Bosnia was part of the same trend in geopolitical sense, because what we have here is an expert in geopolitics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No, sorry, Mr. Tolimir. He is not an expert. He is a witness. Nearly ever answer we have received from the witness is introduced with the words "it's a well-known fact." If that is a well-known fact, you know that already. I -- my proposal is to have our first break now. You may consider this situation with your Legal Advisor, and we will resume five minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I would like to remind you and to read out to you the legal background for cross-examination, the legal basis, concerning the discussion we had before the break. We should foremost rely on the applicable law. In our Rules of Procedure and Evidence, Rule 90(H)(i), and I would like to read that out to you, there's the guidance, the legal guidance, for the cross-examining party. I quote: "Cross-examination shall be limited to the subject-matter of the evidence-in-chief and matters affecting the credibility of the witness and, where the witness is able to give evidence relevant to the case for the cross-examining party, to the subject matter of that case." Mr. Tolimir, the last questions, in my view, went far beyond the scope of the testimony of this witness. If you want to put your case about the reasons -- about the reasons of the war or the wars in the former Yugoslavia, you should consider the possibility to call an expert witness during the Defence case, expert witness for history, military background, or political background, and then the Chamber will consider your position. This witness is not an expert witness. This witness, Mr. Petrovic, is a journalist, and he was called by the Prosecution to explain the video footage we have seen in court and which he produced. You should bear that in mind, that this was the scope of the examination-in-chief. The witness might have a strong opinion about many things in relation to the events in the former Yugoslavia, but it's not helpful for your case and for your Defence if you only receive answers with the wording "it is a well-known fact." You need evidence in your case, and you should try to get evidence from the witness and not an opinion. Please bear that in mind and continue your cross-examination, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. On page 14424, line 25, during the direct examination, Mr. Vanderpuye stated or, rather, asked the witness to say something about geopolitics of energy. And on that occasion the witness talked about the geopolitics of water, food, and energy. And he said that it has to do with future. He also mentioned 60 per cent resources. On page 11 of direct examination --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I would like -- may I interrupt you for a moment. I would like to have the page 14424 on the screen, if that is possible.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Do you have the line, Mr. Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Lines 8 to 11 was the question, and then 11 to 25 is the answer. I could also refer you to the previous page, page 11, where the witness said that he was in charge of a centre for political studies. This forms the basis for my questions. It was part of the direct examination. But I accept your guidance. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Just to clarify, on line 11 of page 14424, the last question of Mr. Vanderpuye was: "What does this discipline concern?" One could interpret this as a question of -- in relation to the background and the knowledge and the scientific background of the witness, and not a question about the knowledge he has about certain factors and historical events. That might be a difference. But you said you will continue according to the guidance you have received. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Dr. Petrovic, thank you for all the answers you gave, especially to the ones you gave to the questions I put to you. It's unfortunate that you couldn't answer all my questions. Thank you for coming here. God bless you on your return home. God bless you and your family. And I hope your research will be fruitful, your research and of your centre.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, those were the questions of the Defence for this witness. We don't have any further questions. And we wish him a happy return to his home and God-speed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Vanderpuye, do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I do. With your leave, I can get started.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, good afternoon to you. You were asked some questions by General Tolimir about Colonel Bunel, in particular the article that you indicated that you would send once have you a chance to obtain it. I don't have the specific page reference handy, but I think you can recall the subject matter of those questions. First, I just want to be clear that we're talking about Colonel Pierre-Henri Bunel. Is that him?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you indicated that the information he provided you, you found to be credible and reliable.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you are aware that Colonel Bunel was imprisoned on the basis that he provided information to the Serbs about NATO military targets?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in this context he was also apparently charged with treason; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In the discussions you had with Colonel Bunel - and I think you indicated this also in cross-examination - the topic of the Islamisation of the Balkans also came up; right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's a position that you share with him, in terms of your views concerning this; is that fair?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in many aspects.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did Colonel Bunel tell you, during the course of your interview with him, that the Islamic terrorism in the Balkans was encouraged in the war and that Washington had an interest in destabilizing that region?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now I have a concern with these kind of questions during the re-examination. You listened to the guidance we gave to Mr. Tolimir about the scope of his cross-examination and the concern I had to express. You should try to avoid to go into the same field of -- yeah, opinions.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I only have one other question and it is related, obviously, to this same topic, and then I'll move on to another -- to another area. I'm not sure if I got an answer to my last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No, you didn't because I expressed my concern about the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: Did you discuss with Colonel Bunel during your interview with him the idea that there was a basis for concern about the American presence in Europe and the danger, as he saw it, of the Islamisation of the Balkans as a threat to the region?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me remind you, first of all, that there were two interviews. We are talking about the second one which was not done in person but via e-mail. I sent him questions, he sent me answers back. However, he wrote some books. I can't give you the exact titles, but what are you talking about now is something that is contained in those books. And it contains his opinion about the danger of Islamisation of the region and the role of NATO and the USA.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. And that's something that you discussed with him in the course of these e-mails or in person; right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In our first encounter in Paris we discussed these things. I can provide both interviews to you. But in the second interview, as I said, we only -- he only gave me responses. We didn't have any kind of discussion. And in his responses, he did make mention of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. When you were in the Srebrenica area on the 13th and 14th of July, 1995, when you filmed the women on the buses and the men being separated, or the men and the women being removed from Potocari, these aren't the radical Islamists you were talking about during the course of your cross-examination; right? These people that were removed from Potocari that you filmed aren't the radical Islamists that you refer to during the course of your testimony; right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are right. I did not see any Islamists at that time. Those were the people either from Srebrenica or the refugees who had come to Srebrenica when the war started. So those were the people from Bosnia. Bosnians.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Bosnians.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You mentioned during your cross-examination that the information that Bunel provided you concerning fighters that showed up in Tuzla in 1996, I believe you said, that there was some possibility or probability that they were on the list of misting, and I just want to ask you a couple of questions about that. Did you, during your interview or e-mail conversation with Mr. -- Colonel Bunel, come across any information, such as a name, date of birth, place of residence, any biographical information that would enable you to determine whether or not the individuals he spoke about could be on the list of missing in 2011, that we're in now?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, not at all. He never went into any details of that nature. He confined himself to the fact that he had seen a large group of exhausted fighters in the American base in Tuzla. He probably knew a little more, but I wouldn't like to guess. So that is all that he told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Now, during your cross-examination, at page 14490 -- well, let's say 491 and 492, you were asked some questions about the Kravica warehouse by General Tolimir, and in particular he asked you about the number of bodies that you estimated that were outside the building. The question was, and this is at page 14492, line 4, and follows some additional introduction that General Tolimir gave: "Can you please tell us whether these were all the bodies which you filled at the location in Kravica or is there another footage? Thank you." And your answer was: "General, all bodies which I personally saw were filmed. But let me repeat once again, my footage hardly lasts 3 seconds. It's a maximum 3 seconds while passing by Kravica." You say you also "shot ... 3 or 4 dead people in Srebrenica itself on the 14th of July, the following day." I want to ask you some questions about that. When you were shooting this footage outside the warehouse, as I recall your testimony, you were on the way to the Bratunac health centre; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as far as my memory serves me.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you never stopped at the Kravica warehouse on the way.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't stop at that particular spot. But we did stop on another location before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And the location you stopped at before that, I think you said, was Sandici. Is that near the meadow where the prisoners were being held?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I have been told later, that that was the name of that topographical feature.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And if I may ask: Who told you that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that this was told me during my first interview with Mr. Nicholls when I made my first statement. However, I'm not sure. Anyway, it came from the Court, because they had detailed maps, and I think I saw the name Sandici on one of those maps as a name of a hamlet. In 2006 I was in the area with a crew from the French television, but I did not recognise any of these places.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And when you drove by the warehouse, were you together with Borovcanin in the vehicle?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the only vehicle that I was in during the 40 hours that I spent in the area, and this car belonged to Ljubisa Borovcanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, was he in it with you when you drove by the warehouse and filmed the footage that the Trial Chamber has seen?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I can remember, we were together in the car, and we travelled as far as the town and the health centre there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you indicated that you had heard that an individual had been -- that one of Borovcanin's men, who I told you yesterday had been identified as Rade Cuteric [Realtime transcript read in error "Cuderic"], had been injured. Was he in the car with you, as well, when you drove past the warehouse?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, I described to you yesterday in very clear terms that he had been wounded before we had reached the place where he got injured and that, in the meantime, another vehicle drove him urgently to the medical centre. So I don't know what it was the aim of your question. As far as I can remember, no injured person was in the car with Ljubisa Borovcanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: How long did it take you to get to the Bratunac health centre from the point that you can see on the video that you were filming? Approximately.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I -- I can't tell you how many minutes. The only way is for the two of us to go there and try to -- and measure the time and also to take into account, when doing so, some interruptions that was due to fighting. It's a short trip, maybe 15 or 20 minutes. But please don't hold me to that, because I have pushed this into back of my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. I just wanted you to estimate it, and I see that you said about 15 or 20 minutes. That's -- that's your recollection. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. But I cannot say that that is an absolute truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. I want to show you 65 ter 3284. And what you can see here is -- this is a transcript of an interview that was conducted with Ljubisa Borovcanin. I think we have it over the 11th and 12th of March, 2002. Let me give you the page number that I want to refer you to.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'd like to go to page 64 in the English. It's 64 not necessarily in e-court, but the page number of the transcript. It should be 59, I believe, in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And here we have Mr. Borovcanin describing the events that you've testified about. And he says -- you'll see the first line that I'll read from is in the second paragraph, AG, that's Allistair Graham, and that's the investigator for the OTP. "The time is still around 1450; we'll continue with the interview." And he says: "So just to clarify, Milos Stupar asked you to return to his location and this is what you do?" And we have Borovcanin answer as follows: "So I passed Sandici where we parted ... nothing was going on in that area. I continued. So I continued down the road and I reached the building of agricultural association of some kind in Kravica. And I saw police officers that were previously placed along the road. I saw them gathered there. I saw Lukic's unit. They were all together as well, and I saw a large number of bodies of people that were killed in the yard belonging to that Zadruga. It was not clear to me what happened, so I asked Stupar what happened. So, briefly, he informed me that a military unit brought this large number of prisoners from Sandici to that place. So, as they were entering the backyard or the yard, one Muslim tried to grab someone's gun, and as the Muslim grabbed the gun, he killed the police officer. And then Cuteric, who was a deputy commander of that unit ..." And we'll have to go down a little bit. "So he grabbed the barrel of the gun by that Muslim so the shooting continued and Officer Cuteric, he was injured because he grabbed that hot barrel and his -- both palms were burnt to the bone. And the shooting started after that. The military unit that brought those Muslims there, they started shooting and then, you know, mass killings occurred. And ... I asked Stupar, What was the role of the police and all that?" We'll have to go to the next page in the English. "And he said that the police officers did not participate in the shooting." He then says: "I placed Cuteric, who was injured, in the car. I took him to the health centre in Bratunac and then he received medical assistance because no other vehicles were available." So my question to you, first, is: Can you reconcile what you've told us with what you can see Borovcanin, who was with you at the time, has said concerning the events surrounding Kravica warehouse? First, can you tell us, do you now recall whether you stopped at the warehouse?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, there is nothing for me to reconcile. I do not have any memory of any injured person being in the car. This is why in the text, the interview in the magazine, I think, mentioned the whole story which I heard rather than saw, because is it not strange for you that in all the footage which I shot, including the group of the dead, it's illogical that there is a wounded man in the car because there is no sequence including him? So Mr. Borovcanin and myself seem to be at complete odds when it comes to what we remember. I do not remember any wounded combatant in his car, nor that we ever stopped there in Kravica. There is not a trace of anything like that in my memory, because there would have been some kind of trace in my text. I'm not sure what this is about, but I cannot reconcile these two stories. And I stand by my own. I have no reason to change my position and take this, what has been noted during another interview, as something that is mine. I do not remember it in this way. Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, I'm glad that you've raised it because that is the gist of my question. And the gist of my question is: If we credit what's in this statement by Mr. Borovcanin, whom you've testified was with you throughout, pretty much, the period of time, the 40 hours that you were in and around Bratunac and Srebrenica, then it would seem, or stand to reason, that there would be other footage concerning the Kravica warehouse dead. Let me take you to page 66 in the English and ask you about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: We've have to go to the bottom of the page, line 23 in the English. Let's see if I have it in the B/C/S. I think it's line 8, page 62 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And we'll start there. This is Mr. Borovcanin speaking. He says: "So I've never been to that warehouse and I was standing on the road and that's what I saw because I was on the road. I never went down?" Then the question is from PM, who is Peter McCloskey: "Did you look into the warehouse from the road? And the answer was: "I looked in the direction of the warehouse, and I saw dead people." "Q. I know. Did you look in the warehouse?" And he says, Borovcanin: "So, well, I can tell you that I looked towards the warehouse and Pirocanac was near me." That's you, first of all; right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's my nickname, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Pirocanac was near me and he was taking photographs or he was filming the place, and on that footage you can also see the warehouse but you cannot see what's in the warehouse because it was dark. Here we see Borovcanin referring to you taking photographs or filming the place. And he says, immediately before that, he hadn't been to the warehouse but he was standing on the road. How do you reconcile what he said here with what appears in your three seconds of footage?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, after 16 years, or even 12 or 10, these are obviously two different testimonies. But I have a principle of mine. I have been a journalist for a long time, and what I filmed in passing, that was it. I do not remember those memories of Mr. Borovcanin nor did I ever discuss this with him. I had this broadcast on TV immediately. So the materials reached Studio B immediately, and I wasn't the only one who saw them. I included absolutely everything that was interesting from the point of view of war, the dynamics of war operations, and so on and so forth. So from the footage itself, the three seconds, one can see that it was shot from a car that was moving. And, really, most sincerely, I cannot remember something that would probably suit you better, that I ever stopped there with him for a single second. I really do not remember that. It is certain that there would be more, because if there were the 20 dead, I suppose I would have filmed others if I had seen them. First of all, yesterday I heard the question "How many doors were there?" I didn't see the door at all. Whether they were locked or unlocked, you have to realize that I was filming in the zone which was under fire, where operations were still underway, and I absolutely don't remember us stopping. That is my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. I have your answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to tender this transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 3284 shall be assigned Exhibit P2235. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have nothing against Mr. Vanderpuye asking the witness everything, but this extends beyonds the limits of the additional examination. During the cross-examination, I only said what was asked during the examination-in-chief, namely that the camera recorded what was recorded during the three seconds. And please, if this could be taken into account from this point onwards and that the questions should not extend beyond the scope of the cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Vanderpuye, can you give us a reference?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, I can. I thought I did. Maybe I misspoke. I referred to page 14492 of the transcript, where General Tolimir asked

utterances.speaker: DR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: "Can you please tell us whether these were all the bodies which you filmed at the location in Kravica or is there another footage? And he says: All I filmed was three seconds. And so I've asked him questions concerning his opportunity to film and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed. You gave us the reference earlier. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You have mentioned that during this period of time, Dr. Petrovic, you were under fire. I'd like to show you 65 ter 7398. This is a composite photograph from the footage that we saw yesterday during the course of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: As you recall, when we ran the footage yesterday, I indicated to you that there were three men, apparently soldiers, on this video that did not appear to be ducking for cover or were trying to avoid being fired on at the time that you filmed this footage. And you provided an answer concerning that. Now you said, essentially, that you were under fire at the time and wouldn't, as I understand it, have had an opportunity to film more of what we can see here, including the bodies that are piled up in front of the doors and the goings-on at the time. You've also described this particular scene as perhaps some of the most jarring or shocking footage you've ever filmed. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in terms of the intensity of impression at the moment of filming this. But thinking now, in the courtroom, and then and there is not one and the same thing. And have to realize the basic thing: I'm holding the camera in this position - please have a look at me. So I'm looking through the lens. I'm not a professional cameraman who would probably have seen more than me, if this is what you're aiming at. I'm a dilettante with a camera of 8-millimetres, and I have limited opportunities. It's 1, 2, 3. So how can I discuss it with you? I would probably try to make a close-up if we had stopped, because this is what a journalist would try to make, a close-up of this horrible scene. Please realize that on this road from the Sandici, where we were going from, until close to Bratunac there were shoot-outs occasionally. Everyone was shooting at everyone else and in such a situation I was filming this, and you expect more from me than this. That's really not fair. I exposed my life so that you would have these images here today. Please allow me. I realize this as a slight provocation on your part. Twice or at least three times in my life, I know this for sure, that there were orders issued to liquidate me because of these -- of this footage, because of this reportage. And I know that once a man whom I don't know personally whose name is General Mladic saved my life by ending this operation, and the other one was a paramilitary commander Arkan, when they learned that somebody from Bosnia said, Liquidate Pirocanac. And now you want me to say more than what I did see. This could have been omitted from the report. I have been exposed to horrible lies and pressure for 15 years. I cannot stand this to the end of my life. I did this honestly, by risking my own life, there, on the ground, and later on, when I learned this, I was a target. I was to be killed. So please do not try to extract more from me than what I already said. I'm really not a man who is afraid of anyone, who has to hide anything, or who is dishonest.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Maybe can you tell us, then, Dr. Pirocanac -- I mean Petrovic, maybe you can tell us, then, why this particular footage doesn't appear on the raw footage that you provided to the Office of the Prosecutor in 2006, I believe it was. This footage appears on the Studio B footage, as we've seen, but it doesn't appear on the raw footage that you used to prepare the Studio B footage that you provided to the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Vanderpuye, you're talking about 2006. Since July 1995, I behaved quite unprofessionally as regards this. I will take you to dinner if you give me an example of such conduct of a journalist who would provide the raw materials to whoever asked to have them. And journalists from around the world who were in Belgrade at the time asked me to provide this to them. A good analysis of my 8-millimetre video cassette indicates that there are several other details which have nothing to do with Srebrenica. It was, first of all, used many times. And in real journalism the principle is that you should use one video cassette only once, and this one was used many times. There is also an image of Karadzic speaking in the TV studio in Pale at one point, which has nothing to do with Srebrenica. So I have given it to everyone, and I was not money oriented at all. I provided all colleagues from across the world with this, to the Dutch and the French and the Americans' TV stations. It passed through many hands. So that it is unfair to express an interest in -- to why is it in the original and not in the raw materials. Well, I guess the original, thanks to which you have this footage, is more interesting. And who were are all the parties that intervened in this? That's something I really cannot know. It's much more important that you have the white house and the hangar, because three seconds is more than zero seconds. If I had had more, I would have used it, because the images I have in the report are poor. And I'm telling you, you keep forgetting that I'm not a cameraman. These are two quite different professions. A journalist's eye views differently than the eye of a cameraman. I was forced to film this because perhaps I was aware of the historic importance of the materials. And for years you have been exploiting it thanks to my own personal risk. I was not insured as the Western journalists are. I was crazy to have exposed my physical integrity in order to film this report so that later on everyone would be attacking me. And don't forget, I have been attacked in Belgrade by the anti-war sector, so to speak, and also by the Bosnian Serbs, and also on several occasions, I'm certain about two, and I know a third journalist in Belgrade who told me that they waited for me at the border. They waited for me to appear, the Bosnian Serbs. So I was supposed to be liquidated physically. You're not taking that into account at all, and I'm asking you, please, as a human, to do that, because I risked a lot in order to film this.
